sections.b: Titus is the shortest of the three Pastoral Letters: three chapters, 46 verses. It has three movements. Chapter 1 sets up leaders: elders for every town of Crete, and a warning against teachers who are upsetting households. Chapter 2 gives each group in the household its duties and grounds them in the grace that "has appeared". Chapter 3 turns to life among outsiders and gives the letter's second great summary of salvation (3:4-7), then closes with travel plans. Its key words are "sound", "sensible", "good works" and "Savior".

Titus is close to 1 Timothy in purpose: both instruct a delegate to set a church in order. It shares the Pastorals' key words, "sound teaching" (1:9; 2:1), "godliness" (1:1; 2:12), the "appearing" (2:13), God "our Savior" (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and "This saying is trustworthy" (3:8). Its list for overseers (1:5-9) differs from 1 Timothy 3 in ways that fit a new church: no rule against recent converts, and elders and overseer named as one. It also has the clearest statements in the three letters of salvation by mercy (3:4-7) and of Christ as "our great God and Savior" (2:13).

The letter shows Titus left on Crete to appoint elders and correct false teachers (1:5, 13), to teach every group in the house churches (2:1-10), and then to hand over to Artemas or Tychicus and join Paul at Nicopolis for the winter (3:12). It calls him Paul's "true-born child in the faith we hold in common" (1:4). Later manuscripts add a note naming him the first overseer of the church of Crete, and Eusebius records the same tradition (Church History 3.4.6).

sections.h: Paul's letter to Titus on Crete
sections.b: The letter assumes churches in many towns of Crete (1:5) and a mission there that Acts does not record. It quotes a Cretan "prophet": "Cretans are always liars, wicked beasts, lazy bellies" (1:12), a line also found in Callimachus and later ascribed to Epimenides. It names opponents "from the circumcision" (1:10), which fits Philo's report of Jewish communities on the island (Embassy to Gaius 282).

sections.h: Paul in the letter to Titus
sections.b: Titus presents Paul as "a slave of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ" (1:1), free, traveling, and planning a winter at Nicopolis (3:12), after a stay on Crete that Acts does not record. On the traditional view Paul wrote it after his release from the imprisonment of Acts 28; on the view of most critical scholars a follower wrote it with the two letters to Timothy, and it shows how Paul was remembered: as the guardian of "sound teaching" and a leader who set churches in order. It is the only letter in which Paul calls himself "a slave of God".

sections.h: Elders and the overseer on Crete
sections.b: Titus is told to "appoint elders town by town" (1:5), and the next verses call the same leader "the overseer" (1:7). Most readers take the two words as one office here, as in Acts 20:17, 28. Chrysostom says "he is speaking of Bishops"; Calvin, that there is "no distinction between a presbyter and a bishop". Churches with bishops answer that the terms had not yet settled. The list of qualities stresses marriage, children, temper, drink, money, hospitality and a firm hold on sound teaching, and it differs from 1 Timothy 3 in leaving out "not a recent convert".

Titus 3:5 says God saved us "through the bath of new birth and the renewing by the Holy Spirit". Most readers since the early church have seen baptism here: the Catechism of the Catholic Church calls baptism "the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit", citing this verse (1215), Chrysostom calls baptism "the laver of regeneration", and Luther's Small Catechism quotes Titus 3. Calvin had "no doubt" the verse alludes to baptism but denied that salvation lies in the water. Baptists read the washing as the Spirit's inner work, which baptism pictures.

The word for "new birth" in Titus 3:5, palingenesia, appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in Matthew 19:28, where it is the rebirth of the world: "when the world is born again". Titus applies it to the believer, washed and renewed by the Spirit. The two uses together suggest that personal new birth is a first share in the renewal of all things.

Titus 2:11-12 pictures grace as a teacher: God's grace "has appeared, with salvation for all people. It trains us to deny ungodliness". Grace here is not only pardon but the power that forms a new life between Christ's first coming and his appearing in glory. In 3:7 believers are "justified by that grace of his".

Titus 3:5-7 states the Pauline pattern briefly: God saved us "not on the basis of works we ourselves had done in righteousness, but in keeping with his mercy", so that, "justified by that grace of his", we would become heirs. It does not speak of "works of the law" as Romans and Galatians do, but of works in general, and it insists just as strongly on good works as the fruit (3:8, 14).

Titus 2:13 speaks of "the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ". On Granville Sharp's rule (1798), one article governing "God" and "Savior" makes them one person, and most modern translations read it so; the King James Version allows two persons, and the New World Translation reads two. Calvin reports that the Arians used the two-person reading; Chrysostom preached on the verse against those who said the Son is less than the Father. Titus 3:4-6 names God our Savior, the Holy Spirit and Jesus Christ our Savior together in one act of salvation.

common: Titus 2:13 calls Jesus "our great God and Savior".
uncommon: Titus 2:13 speaks of two persons, the Father as "the great God" and Jesus as "our Savior".

sections.b: Titus 2:13 is one of a handful of New Testament verses that may call Jesus "God" directly, with John 1:1, John 20:28, Romans 9:5, Hebrews 1:8 and 2 Peter 1:1. The grammar (one article for two nouns) favors one person. The letter also gives Jesus the title "our Savior" in the same places where it gives it to God (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6).

Titus speaks of Christ's return as an "appearing" (epiphaneia), the word for a god or ruler showing himself in public. Grace has already "appeared" (2:11), and believers wait to welcome "the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" (2:13). The Christian life is lived between the two appearings.

sections.h: Titus 2: duties by age and status
sections.b: Titus 2:1-10 groups its duties by age and status: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, slaves. Unlike Ephesians and Colossians it says nothing to husbands, fathers or masters. Three purpose clauses face outward: so that God's word is not insulted (2:5), so that an opponent has nothing bad to say (2:8), so that slaves make the teaching beautiful (2:10). The code is then grounded in grace (2:11-14).

Titus tells slaves to submit to their masters, please them, not talk back and not skim anything off, "so that in all things they make the teaching of God our Savior beautiful". It addresses slaves as moral agents whose conduct adorns the gospel, but it gives no word to masters, unlike Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1. How the churches have read such passages, and how their judgment of slavery changed, is set out on the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon 1:15-16.

Titus 2:3-4 calls older women "teachers of what is good" and gives them the task of teaching the younger women. Some read this as the limit of women's teaching (women teaching women); others note that it is a recognized teaching role, and that Titus himself is told to teach the younger men but not the younger women. The passage is read alongside 1 Timothy 2:11-15, where a card sets out the churches' positions.

Titus 2:5 asks young wives to submit to their own husbands, "so that the word of God is not insulted". The stated reason faces outward. Those who hold to male headship read the command as lasting; others read the reason as mission strategy in the Roman household. Pius XI allowed that a wife's subjection "in its degree and manner may vary according to the different conditions of persons, place and time" (Casti Connubii 28); John Paul II read the New Testament's submission texts as "mutual subjection out of reverence for Christ" (Mulieris Dignitatem 24); the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 says a wife is "to submit herself graciously to the servant leadership of her husband".

"Remind them to submit to rulers and authorities and obey them" (Titus 3:1) repeats the teaching of Romans 13:1, with the same verb and the same word for "authorities" (Titus adds "rulers"), for believers on Roman-ruled Crete. The command comes with no explanation, which suggests it was standard teaching, and it is joined to gentleness toward all people (3:2).

Titus describes "many who are unruly, who talk nonsense and lead minds astray, especially those from the circumcision" (1:10). They teach in homes for money (1:11), spread "Jewish myths" and human commands (1:14), purity rules (1:15), genealogies and fights about the law (3:9). The response is correction (1:9, 13), refusal to argue endlessly (3:9), and, for a divisive person, two warnings and then separation (3:10).

Titus 1:10 singles out "those from the circumcision", the phrase Galatians 2:12 uses for Jewish believers who pressed for keeping the law. On Crete they seem to have taught "Jewish myths", human commands and purity rules (1:14-15). The letter does not mention circumcision as a demand, and its answer is about purity: "All things are clean to those who are clean".

sections.h: Titus, uncircumcised, and "those from the circumcision"
sections.b: Titus was the Greek coworker whom Paul took to Jerusalem, and "not even he was made to get circumcised" (Galatians 2:3). It is fitting that the letter bearing his name warns against "those from the circumcision" (Titus 1:10).

sections.h: "All things are clean to those who are clean"
sections.b: Titus 1:15 answers teachers of purity rules with the principle of Jesus and Paul: what makes a person unclean is inside. Compare Mark 7:19, "(With this he made all foods clean.)", and Romans 14:20, "All things are clean". The opponents' "minds and consciences are stained". Chrysostom: things are "not clean or unclean from their own nature, but from the disposition of him who partakes of them".

Titus 1:15 says the opponents' "minds and consciences are stained": the inner judge itself is polluted and can no longer be trusted. The Pastorals speak of the conscience often, as good (1 Timothy 1:5, 19) or seared (1 Timothy 4:2).

Titus 1:8 puts hospitality first among the overseer's positive qualities, and the letter ends with a case of it: Titus is to send Zenas and Apollos on their way "so that they are short of nothing" (3:13). Traveling believers depended on such homes.

The elder must be "the husband of one wife" (Titus 1:6; also 1 Timothy 3:2, 12). Readings: no polygamy; no remarriage after divorce; no second marriage at all; faithfulness to one's wife; being married. Chrysostom read it both as honoring marriage and as excluding a man who had married twice, and one thirteenth-century manuscript (460) even adds a rule against ordaining the twice-married. Titus 2:4-5 also speaks of young wives who love their husbands and children.

Titus 3:9 tells Titus to keep away from "foolish debates, genealogies, quarrels and fights about the law", which "do no good and lead nowhere". With 1 Timothy 1:4 ("myths and endless genealogies"), it suggests speculation built on the Bible's lists of ancestors, perhaps tied to the "Jewish myths" of Titus 1:14.

Titus uses the vocabulary of Greek ethics: eusebeia "godliness" (1:1), sōphrōn "sensible" (1:8; 2:2-6, 12), philanthrōpia "love for humankind" (3:4), and the triad "sensibly, rightly and in a godly way" (2:12). It also quotes a Greek poet (1:12). The letter takes the best words of its culture and grounds them in grace and the cross (2:11-14).
In Titus 3:13 Apollos is on the road again with Zenas the lawyer, and Titus is to send them on "so that they are short of nothing". It is the last mention of Apollos in the New Testament.
Paul plans to send Artemas or Tychicus to Crete so that Titus can come to him at Nicopolis (Titus 3:12). Since 2 Timothy 4:12 says Tychicus was sent to Ephesus, some suppose Artemas went to Crete.

Titus 2:14 describes Christ's work in Israel's words: to "redeem" from all lawless deeds (the Greek of Psalm 130:8), to "make clean" a people (Ezekiel 37:23), "his own private treasure" (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6). Promises made to Israel are applied to a church of Jews and Gentiles. Readers differ on whether this means sharing, inheriting or replacing Israel's calling.
sections.refs: Titus 2:14; Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Ezekiel 37:23; Psalm 130:8; 1 Peter 2:9

sections.b: Titus 2:14 sums up the cross as self-giving with a purpose: Christ "gave himself up on our behalf, so that he could redeem us", using the verb lytroō, of the same family as "ransom" in Mark 10:45. The purpose is moral as well as legal: a cleansed people, "eager for good works".

Titus 3:5-6 speaks of "the renewing by the Holy Spirit", whom God "poured out on us in rich measure through Jesus Christ", using Joel's verb (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). The passage names Father, Spirit and Son together in one saving act.

"As for a person who causes splits, give him a first and a second warning, and then turn him away" (Titus 3:10). The word is hairetikos, the root of "heretic", but here it means a maker of factions. The process resembles Matthew 18:15-17. Later churches built heavier measures on the verse than it states.

sections.h: God our Savior, Christ our Savior
sections.b: Titus calls God "our Savior" three times (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and Jesus Christ "our Savior" three times (1:4; 2:13; 3:6). God's grace "has appeared, with salvation for all people" (2:11), and God "saved us" in mercy, through the bath of new birth (3:5).

Titus 3:5 sets mercy against works: God saved us "not on the basis of works we ourselves had done in righteousness, but in keeping with his mercy". Mercy here is joined with God's "kindness" and "love for humankind" (3:4).
The overseer must not be "a heavy drinker" (paroinos, Titus 1:7), and older women must not be "enslaved to a lot of wine" (2:3). The concern is wine's control over a person, not wine itself.
